name: Purple Rain (1984)
teaser: Prince wrote it as a guitar showcase and the film's concert scene is a real performance — the solo at the end is a single unedited take, and the song's gospel choir is the 'rain' made sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the full nine minutes with the solo — it's one unedited take. The song's genius is that the grief is the guitar; the lyrics are the weather.

name: Hotel California (1976)
teaser: The song's lyrics were written as a literal road trip gone wrong — the 'you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave' line is the song's thesis, and the famous dual guitar solo was improvised.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the dual guitar outro — two solos trading phrases. The song's genius is that the hotel is a metaphor you can't pin down; the ambiguity is the point.

name: Sweet Child o' Mine (1987)
teaser: The riff started as a string-skipping warm-up exercise that Slash called a joke — Axl wrote the lyrics in five minutes about his girlfriend, and the song became the band's biggest hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the intro and notice the 'joke' riff — the warm-up became the hook. The song's genius is that the guitar solo is a conversation with the vocal.

name: Creep (1992)
teaser: The band hated the song and nearly left it off the album — it became their only mainstream hit, and the 'special' lyric is about Thom Yorke's real crush at university.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the quiet-loud structure — the verse is a whisper, the chorus is a scream. The song's genius is that the self-loathing is the hook.

name: Seven Nation Army (2003)
teaser: The iconic riff is a bass line played on a guitar with a pitch-shifter — Jack White wrote it while touring and the 'seven nation army' was his phrase for the US military draft.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the riff and notice it's a guitar pretending to be a bass. The song's genius is that the riff carries the whole song; the lyrics are the counter-melody.

name: Dancing Queen (1976)
teaser: Written for the Swedish king's wedding, the song's 'young and sweet, only seventeen' line was about a real 17-year-old who danced at a club ABBA visited — it's the only song ABBA wrote for a woman.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the piano intro and the key change — the song is engineered joy. The song's genius is that the disco beat is the 'dance' made literal.

name: Superstition (1972)
teaser: Stevie wrote the drum groove first — the 'superstition' lyrics came after, and the song's famous clavinet riff is played on a real Hohner Clavinet through a wah pedal.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the clavinet — it's the song's engine. The song's genius is that the groove is the thesis; the lyrics are the afterthought that made it a hit.

name: Comfortably Numb (1979)
teaser: The two guitar solos were recorded by two different guitarists (David Gilmour twice, years apart) — the song's lyrics are about Roger Waters' stage collapse and the doctor who injected him.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the two solos — the first is distant, the second is the climax. The song's genius is that the numbness is the narrator and the music is the feeling.

name: Don't Stop Believin' (1981)
teaser: The song flopped on release and became a hit years later through karaoke — the 'streetlight people' lyric is about real people in a real Detroit club, and the song's key change is its famous kick.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the key change before the final chorus — it's the song's ignition. The song's genius is that the 'believin'' is the instruction.

name: Crazy in Love (2003)
teaser: The horn sample is from a 1970s Chi-Lites song and the 'uh oh' hook was improvised — Beyoncé's debut solo hit was written in a studio with Jay-Z in two days.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the horn sample and the 'uh oh' — both are the hooks. The song's genius is that the horns are the chaos; the beat is the control.

name: I Will Survive (1978)
teaser: Written as the B-side after the label demanded a song about Gaynor's real injury — the 'survive' anthem became the first disco song to top the charts after disco's fall, a comeback in itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the string section and the spoken intro — the song is a speech. The song's genius is that the defiance is the hook; the 'survive' is the thesis.

name: London Calling (1979)
teaser: Written as a warning about the Thames flooding London — the band predicted the 'ice age' of climate change 40 years early, and the song's bassline is its most copied riff.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the bassline and the flood imagery — the warning is real. The song's genius is that the punk rage is a prophecy.

name: Bohemian Rhapsody (1975)
teaser: Freddie Mercury wrote most of it on the piano in his flat and the label refused to release a six-minute song with no chorus — it became one of the best-selling singles ever. The 'Galileo' backing vocals took three weeks to layer.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen with headphones and count the distinct sections — it's opera, ballad and hard rock in one track. Then listen for the multitracked 'Galileo' pile-up that takes the song to its peak.

name: Smells Like Teen Spirit (1991)
teaser: Kurt Cobain wrote the riff after mishearing a friend's slogan about a deodorant, and the band was sure it would flop — the music video's bored-mascot chaos made MTV viewers think the crowd was real.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the verse dynamics — it's the quiet-loud formula that ended an era of hair metal. Then watch the music video and notice the mascot's eyes: the apathy is the point.

name: Billie Jean (1982)
teaser: The bassline was built from a drum machine demo Quincy Jones wanted to cut, and the 'Not my lover' lyric was about a real fan's claim. The video broke MTV's color barrier in 1983.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the bassline first — it's the whole song's engine, and Jackson's vocal enters over it like a second instrument. Then count the empty beats in the intro: the tension is the hook.

name: Imagine (1971)
teaser: Lennon wrote it at his piano in Tittenhurst Park with Yoko watching, and the white room in the video is that actual house. It's the most-performed protest song of the 20th century without a single angry note.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the spare arrangement — just piano, voice and a string sweep that enters late. The radicalism is in how quiet it is; the 'no possessions' line lands because nothing is shouted.

name: Like a Rolling Stone (1965)
teaser: Dylan nearly shelved the six-minute draft as a novel fragment, and a session drummer's organ figure became the most famous riff in rock. It's the song that made pop lyrics literary.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the organ — it enters like a second voice answering every line. The song's question ('how does it feel?') is asked to the listener, not the subject.

name: Stairway to Heaven (1971)
teaser: The band kept it off singles for years so the album would sell, and the famous 'guitar store' ban was born from butchered covers. The recorder solo was played on a Mellotron, not real flutes.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen through headphones and track the volume arc — it's a quiet-to-loud journey in one song. The 'ooh-ooh' before the solo is the song's center of gravity.

name: Yesterday (1965)
teaser: Paul McCartney dreamed the melody and wrote the working title 'Scrambled Eggs' before settling on lyrics — it's the most-covered song ever, with over 2,200 recorded versions.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the string quartet — it was the first Beatles song to use classical instruments. The melody is so natural it feels inevitable; try to hear it without the violins and it loses half its sadness.

name: Hallelujah (1984)
teaser: Cohen wrote dozens of verses over five years — the song's famous 'secret chord' is a David reference, and it flopped on release before Jeff Buckley's 1994 cover made it immortal.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Buckley version after the Cohen original and hear how the same words change meaning with a different voice. The song is about broken love disguised as scripture.

name: Respect (1967)
teaser: Written by Otis Redding as a man's plea, Aretha flipped the pronouns and demanded it — her version became a civil-rights and feminist anthem, and the 'R-E-S-P-E-C-T' spelling was her idea.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the spelling section — it's the song's thesis in letters. Then notice how the backing singers answer every line: the call-and-response is the argument.

name: Purple Haze (1967)
teaser: Hendrix said the lyric came from a dream about walking under the sea — the famous opening riff is a tritone, the 'devil's interval' banned in medieval church music.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff and hear the tritone — it's deliberately unsettling. Then notice how the solo bends the same interval back into melody.

name: What a Wonderful World (1967)
teaser: Satchmo recorded it at 66, and the label shelved it for a year — it only charted in the US after being used in a film. The song was written as an antidote to Vietnam-era cynicism.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Armstrong's voice — recorded after his throat problems, it's the sound of a man who knows the world isn't wonderful and sings anyway. The trumpet at the end is his own instrument replying.

name: Thriller (1982)
teaser: The 14-minute video cost more than most films of the era and the song's famous Vincent Price rap was recorded in two takes — the werewolf howl is a real wolf recording.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the Vincent Price rap at the end — it's horror as pop. The song's bassline is the horror; the video just makes it visible.

name: Every Breath You Take (1983)
teaser: Sting wrote it in Jamaica after a divorce, and was horrified to realize people thought it romantic — it's a song about surveillance, not love, and it's one of the most-played songs ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the lyrics as a threat, not a promise — the stalker's logic is the song. The bass is the heartbeat; the song never resolves the tension.

name: My Heart Will Go On (1997)
teaser: James Horner wrote the theme secretly because the director hated songs in his films — Celine recorded it in one take, and the 'Titanic' flute is actually a synthesized penny whistle.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the synthesized whistle — it's not a real instrument. The song's melody was built from a demo Horner kept hidden; the director only heard it after the film was cut.

name: Shape of You (2017)
teaser: Sheeran wrote it about his girlfriend in 10 minutes, and the marimba riff was sampled from a demo he made with a toy. It became the most-streamed song on Spotify's history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the marimba — it's the song's memory hook, and the verse's rhythmic switch ('the club isn't the best place') is the same riff in disguise. The song is a loop wearing a narrative.

name: Blinding Lights (2019)
teaser: The Weeknd wanted a song that sounded like 'Take On Me' and 'It's All Coming Back to Me Now' — the 1980s synthwave production made it the most-streamed song in Spotify history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the drum machine and the synth arpeggio — they're pure 1980s. The song's loneliness is hidden under the dance beat; the 'I can't see clearly' line is literal in the video.

name: Old Town Road (2019)
teaser: Made with a $30 beat from a teenager on YouTube, the song was removed from the country charts and Billy Ray Cyrus joined a remix — it spent 19 weeks at #1, a record.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the banjo over the trap beat — the genre clash is the point. The song's viral life is its real story; the remix with Cyrus is the chapter that made it history.

name: Royals (2013)
teaser: Lorde wrote the hook after seeing a photo of a Royals baseball cap, and the label nearly cut the track — the minimal production was the 16-year-old's rebellion against opulent pop.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for what's NOT there — the song has almost no bass and no chorus explosion. The minimalism is the message: luxury is the absence of need.

name: Rolling in the Deep (2010)
teaser: Adele wrote it in 10 minutes after a breakup, and the stomping percussion was recorded by stamping on a floor — the 'gonna make you love me' threat is the whole song.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the stomp — it's a foot on a wooden floor, and it IS the beat. The song's anger is in the restraint; the key change at the end is a door slamming.

name: Uptown Funk (2014)
teaser: Bruno Mars and Ronson wrote it after a week of funk references — the bassline was built from Chic's 'Good Times' and the horns were recorded live in a Nashville studio.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the bassline — it's a direct descendant of 1970s funk. The song's genius is that it sounds improvised but every fill is placed; count the horn stabs.

name: Wonderwall (1995)
teaser: Noel Gallagher wrote it about a friend, not a lover, and the song's five-chord pattern became the acoustic-guitar standard of a generation — it's one of the most-covered songs of the 1990s.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the 'maybe' that starts the chorus — it's the song's engine. The song is a promise that never lands; the narrator doesn't know if the wall will break either.

name: Lose Yourself (2002)
teaser: Eminem wrote the hook in the studio bathroom during the filming of 8 Mile — the song's 'one shot' theme is literally about the take he was about to film.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — the record scratch and the first verse are a single breath. The song's anxiety is the point: the palm-sweat moment is the song.

name: Sicko Mode (2018)
teaser: The song is three beats stitched together with no chorus — it was literally made in the studio with producer switch-ups mid-session, and the beat changes are the hook.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the beat switches — there are three, and each one resets the song's momentum. The song's structure is its subject: chaos as composition.

name: Gangnam Style (2012)
teaser: The first YouTube video to pass a billion views — PSY's 'horse dance' was based on his own actual bad dancing, and the lyrics mock Seoul's wealthy Gangnam district.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the video and notice the satire — the 'rich' scenes are all absurd. The song's joke is that the dancer is neither rich nor cool; the dance is the punchline.

name: Dynamite (2020)
teaser: The first all-Korean-group song to debut at #1 on the Hot 100 — the disco-pop track was released during lockdown and its music video's retro styling is a direct 1970s homage.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the disco strings and the handclaps — the 1970s references are precise. The song's joy is political: a Korean group singing 'light it up like dynamite' in English was a statement.

name: Gangsta's Paradise (1995)
teaser: The song samples Stevie Wonder's 'Pastime Paradise' and was written for a film about gang life — it became one of the best-selling rap singles ever, and Coolio wrote the chorus as a moral warning.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the Stevie Wonder sample — the choir underneath is his original. The song's power is the contrast between the serene sample and the violent verses.

name: Africa (1982)
teaser: The band wrote it as a joke about Westerners romanticizing Africa, and the song's famous backing vocals took hours to record — it became a meme decades later, loved for being sincere.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the kalimba (thumb piano) — it's the song's signature sound, played by the keyboardist who'd never touched one before. The song's earnestness is why the meme works.

name: I Will Always Love You (1973)
teaser: Dolly wrote it as a farewell to her mentor Porter Wagoner and refused to sell the publishing — Whitney's 1992 cover made it one of the best-selling singles ever, and Dolly kept her rights.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Dolly's original first — it's a country ballad, not a power anthem. Then hear Whitney's a cappella opening: the song was always about the space between two people.

name: Jolene (1973)
teaser: The song's melody was inspired by a real girl who flirted with her husband, and the name came from a young fan — Dolly wrote it in one afternoon and the 'pleading' vocal is a country masterclass.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the desperation in the first verse — the narrator doesn't ask, she begs. The song's genius is that Jolene is never described as evil; she's just beautiful, and that's enough.

name: Take On Me (1985)
teaser: The song charted in three different decades and its rotoscope animation video was a technical breakthrough — the band re-recorded it four times over three years before it hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the synth riff — it's one of the most recognizable in pop. The video's sketch-to-real transition is the song made visual: the pencil world is the synth world.

name: Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) (1983)
teaser: The song was built on a $20 drum machine loop and Annie Lennox's iconic video look was a last-minute decision — the band was broke and the label nearly cut them.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the drum machine — it's the whole song's skeleton, and the bassline enters like a third voice. The video's gender-play is the song's real subject: identity as costume.

name: Video Games (2011)
teaser: Made on a laptop in a bedroom and uploaded to YouTube, the song's lo-fi production launched a million imitators — the vintage-film aesthetic was also homemade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the film-sound effects under the vocals — the song was literally scored like a movie. The 'heaven is a place on earth' sample is the ghost in the machine.

name: Somebody That I Used to Know (2011)
teaser: The song's duet structure was inspired by a breakup, and the 'body paint' music video is one continuous shot — the artist spent years away from music after its success.

exploreAction.targetName: Somebody That I Used to Know (2011)
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the two voices — they never sing together, which IS the song. The 'now you're just somebody' line is the thesis; the video's paint makes it literal.

name: Hey Ya! (2003)
teaser: André 3000 wrote a breakup song disguised as a party anthem — the band's 'shake it like a Polaroid' line is a real instruction, and the song's sadness is hidden under pure joy. Hey Ya!

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the key change at the end — it's the song's confession. The funk is the mask; the lyrics are a relationship falling apart in a club.

name: Happy (2013)
teaser: The song was written for a film and rejected, then released as a single — the 24-hour music video was shot in 24 locations with real people dancing, and the claps were recorded in the studio.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the claps — they're the song's heartbeat, recorded by Pharrell's own hands. The song's simplicity is the craft; there's no bridge, just joy.

name: Can't Stop the Feeling! (2016)
teaser: Written for a Trolls movie, the song's disco revival made it the biggest-selling single of 2016 — the 'happy' is engineered, which is exactly the point. Can't Stop the Feeling!

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the falsetto 'nothing can stop me' — it's the song's peak, and it arrives without a build. The song is pure chemical joy; the disco strings are the prescription.

name: Toxic (2003)
teaser: The song's strings were sampled from a Bollywood film and the 'toxic' lyric was Britney's own idea — it's considered one of the greatest pop songs ever by critics.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the Bollywood strings — they're the song's secret weapon. The song's danger is in the beat; the lyrics are the warning label.

name: Umbrella (2007)
teaser: The song was written for Britney Spears, who turned it down — Rihanna's version became her breakthrough, and the 'ella ella' hook was almost cut for being too silly.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the 'ella ella' hook — it's the song's memory engine, and the beat's heartbeat is the rain. The song's promise ('under my umbrella') is the whole story.

name: Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) (2008)
teaser: Beyoncé recorded it in a single day and the choreography was inspired by a 1960s dance troupe — the black-and-white video was shot in one take per angle.

exploreAction.targetName: Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) (2008)
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the video and count the three dancers — the precision is the performance. The song's demand is its power: the ring is the argument.

name: Havana (2017)
teaser: The song's 'Havana, ooh na-na' hook was improvised in the studio, and the video's old-movie aesthetic hides a twist — the song's Cuba longing is real, but the ending is a joke.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the trumpet — it's the song's soul, played by a real session musician. The song is a love letter to a city the singer barely knew; that's the ache.

name: Despacito (2017)
teaser: The Justin Bieber remix made the Spanish-language original the most-streamed song in history — the song's 'despacito' (slowly) is both a tempo and a request.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the original, not the remix — the Spanish phrasing is the song's architecture. The 'despacito' hook is the whole song in one word.

name: Waka Waka (This Time for Africa) (2010)
teaser: Written for the 2010 World Cup, the song's chorus samples a 1980s Cameroonian hit — the dance moves in the video are real African dances.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the sampled Cameroonian guitar — the song is a translation. The 'Waka Waka' hook is a real Tsonga phrase meaning 'do it do it'.

name: Firework (2010)
teaser: Perry wrote it after reading Jack Kerouac's On the Road — the song's 'firework' metaphor was inspired by a real comment from a fan who felt invisible.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the key change before the final chorus — it's the song's ignition. The song's pep talk is engineered, but the engineering is the craft.

name: Born This Way (2011)
teaser: Gaga wrote it as a direct answer to the bullying she survived in school — the song's 'born this way' became a queer anthem and the music video is a birth-to-rebirth allegory.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the spoken opening — it's a sermon, not a verse. The song's radicalism is that it refuses to argue: the self is the fact.

name: All Too Well (2012)
teaser: The 10-minute version's release in 2021 broke records — the song's 'scarf' lyric is famously autobiographical, and the song's real subject is the memory of a memory.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the scarf — it's the song's emotional anchor, and it never comes back. The song's genius is that the narrator can't stop telling the story she's telling.

name: Circles (2019)
teaser: The song's chord progression literally circles — the title is the structure — and the chorus's falsetto was recorded in one take.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the circle — the progression returns to the start, and the song never resolves. The song's trap is that you can't leave a loop you're in.

name: Snooze (2022)
teaser: SZA wrote it about being so in love she can't sleep — the song's 'snooze' is both the state and the excuse, and the album it came from won Album of the Year.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the falsetto 'I'll touch you in the morning' — the promise is the song's core. The production's warmth is the love; the lyrics are the anxiety.

name: Kill Bill (2022)
teaser: The song's revenge fantasy samples a 1980s R&B hit and the video's bridal-gore aesthetic made it a viral moment — the humor is the point, the violence is the joke.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the sampled Diana Ross hook — the sweetness is the contrast. The song's confession ('I might kill my ex') is funny precisely because it's sung so gently.
